title: In weakness and fear (1 Corinthians 2)
hook: Paul came to them trembling, not with clever speeches
tomorrow: two teachers, one church. who gets credit for the growth?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a message that sounds foolish to some, and Paul agreeing. The line: the foolishness of God.

Shaking hands before a recital, a speech, a first day somewhere new. Paul had them too. Here's how he remembers walking into Corinth: "And I was with you in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling." No grand entrance. The man some of them now chant like a team name came to their city nervous. So what did a trembling man decide to say?
screen: `SHAKING HANDS.` → `PAUL ARRIVES TREMBLING.` → `WHAT DID HE DECIDE TO SAY?`

segments.voice: First, what he didn't bring: "And I, brethren, when I came to you, came not with excellency of speech or of wisdom". Then what he chose: "For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified." One subject, on purpose. "And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power". Why come that way? "That your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God." If a great talker had won them over, their faith would lean on the talker: the fan-club problem, solved before it started. Later in the chapter comes a line some readers lift out on its own: "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him." Heard alone, it can sound like heaven someday, hidden for now. But Paul's next words are: "But God hath revealed them unto us by his Spirit." The nervous man with plain words isn't hiding anything. He's saying the depth comes from God, not from the speaker.
screen: `NOT EXCELLENCY OF SPEECH.` · `ONE SUBJECT, ON PURPOSE.` · `FAITH THAT DOESN'T LEAN ON HIM.` · `EYE HATH NOT SEEN, BUT REVEALED.` · then, large: `IN WEAKNESS AND MUCH TREMBLING.`

segments.voice: Write down one thing you need to say soon: a thank-you, an apology, a hard truth. Cross out every word that's there to impress until only the plain sentence is left. Then sit with it, shaky or not.
In weakness and fear. How Paul says he first came to Corinth: trembling, plain-spoken, with one subject.
The line to keep: in weakness and much trembling, and the message still got through. Go gently.

howItsDone: Some preachers and teachers read 1 Corinthians 2:1–5 before they speak, as a reminder to keep their words plain and point beyond themselves.

fork.setup: you're giving a toast at your brother's graduation. you have a clever line and a true one, and you're nervous. what fits 1 Corinthians 2?
options: say the true one plainly, nerves and all.
use the clever line so nobody notices the nerves.
skip the toast until you can do it without shaking.
fork.reveal: Paul came trembling, chose one subject, and kept his speech plain, so what he said wouldn't lean on how he said it.

original.note: Greek: weakness. In 1 Corinthians 2:3: in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling.

chat.says: solo auditions tomorrow. everyone here sounds like a pro. my hands are already shaking. do i even try?
options: Try, shaking and all. Paul came trembling with plain words. Sing it simply, not to impress.
Only if you can stop shaking first. Nerves mean you're not ready yet, honestly.
Try, but pick the flashiest song you know. You need to sound like a pro too.
chat.meaning: Paul came to Corinth in weakness and much trembling, with plain words, so their faith wouldn't lean on a clever speaker.

brethren.meaning: old English for brothers; here, the church's members

excellency.meaning: old word for excellence: polish, impressiveness

enticing.meaning: persuasive, meant to lure or impress

Corinth.meaning: a Greek city whose church Paul wrote to
